candidates.statement: The finding of substantial evidence of effectiveness is necessary but not sufficient for FDA 37 approval. The approval decision also requires a determination that the drug is safe for the 38 intended use and that the benefits outweigh the risks. 4 As such, there must be sufficient safety 39 data for FDA to consider the drug’s safety profile. As all drugs have adverse effects, evaluating 40 whether a drug is safe involves determining whether the benefits of the drug outweigh its risks 41 under the conditions of use defined in labeling. Uncertainties about benefits and risks are also 42 considered when making an approval determination; a drug with greater risks may require a 43 greater magnitude and certainty of benefit to support approval. This benefit-risk assessment 5 and 44 other determinations necessary for approval are outside the scope of this guidance. 45
candidates.context: 3 For the purposes of this guidance, the term drug or drugs refers to human drugs and biological products unless otherwise specified. Sponsors should discuss their anticipated approach to demonstrating substantial evidence of 47 effectiveness with FDA early in development, such as at a pre-investigational new drug 48 application meeting, and no later than at an end-of-phase 2 meeting. 6 When meeting with FDA, 49 sponsors should provide a scientific justification for their proposed approach. Ultimately, 50 whether substantial evidence of effectiveness has been demonstrated will depend on FDA’s 51 review of the marketing application. 52

candidates.statement: Design elements should be selected to help ensure a trial is adequate and well-controlled and can 115 distinguish the effect of the drug from other influences (see section II). Two critical elements are 116 the choice of control 12 and the method of assignment to treatment (e.g., randomization). 117 Generally, the following types of controls are recognized in trials designed to allow for well- 118 supported conclusions about effectiveness: 13 placebo concurrent control, dose-comparison 119 concurrent control, no-treatment concurrent control, active treatment concurrent control, and 120 historical control (a type of external control). Establishing superiority to a randomized 121 concurrent control group (whether an active control or placebo) generally provides strong 122 evidence of effectiveness. 123
candidates.context: Other types of designs can support effectiveness in certain circumstances. For example, designs 125 intended to show non-inferiority (NI) against an active control can be credible and appropriate in 126 situations in which the active control has shown a consistent and large effect in prior superiority 127 trials conducted in a patient population and clinical setting similar to the trial being planned. NI 128 trials provide relevant comparisons against standard of care and can facilitate collection of long- 129 term controlled data to inform the benefit-risk assessment. However, NI trials depend on 130 assumptions about the anticipated effect of the active control in the trial. candidates.statement: There are a variety of important statistical considerations in ensuring that trials are adequate and 209 well-controlled and in evaluating the strength of evidence of effectiveness. 25 An adequate and 210 well-controlled trial should have a prespecified primary analysis that is aligned with a clinically 211 meaningful primary estimand. 26 The traditional approach to limiting erroneous conclusions of 212 effectiveness is to select the design and analysis approach such that the type I error probability 213 with respect to the primary estimand is controlled at a prespecified level. It is common to 214 perform hypothesis testing at a one-sided significance level of 0.025 (or two-sided 0.05), where a 215 p-value or confidence limit is used to determine whether the null hypothesis is rejected in favor 216 of an alternative or is not rejected. In certain settings, such as when the prior evidence for the 217 effectiveness of the drug is not strong, FDA may expect a more stringent prespecified 218 significance level (see section IV.A.2). In settings where regulatory flexibility is warranted, FDA 219 may consider flexibility in the significance level expected (see section V.B.1). Bayesian 220 approaches may also be considered. There should be early communication and agreement with 221 FDA at the design stage on the specification of the prior distribution and the success criteria. 27
candidates.context: C. Trial Analysis Plan 207 The prespecified analysis plan should include appropriate statistical methods. For example, the 224 primary analysis should produce valid estimates and inference for the primary estimand under 225 plausible assumptions 28 and should be prespecified with sufficient detail to allow reproduction of 226 results. Any sources of multiplicity (e.g., multiple doses, multiple primary endpoints) should be 227 handled appropriately. 29 In addition, sensitivity analyses should be planned to explore whether 228 conclusions change under plausible violations in the assumptions of the primary analysis, 229 including missing data assumptions. Supplementary analyses can also be planned to provide 230 further insights into the understanding of the treatment effect. 231

candidates.statement: The overall persuasiveness of a trial’s results can be influenced by many different considerations. 236 These include the magnitude of the p-value (or of alternative measures such as the posterior 237 probability of effectiveness in a Bayesian analysis), as well as the magnitude and clinical 238 meaningfulness of the effect on the primary endpoint. To contribute to a demonstration of 239 substantial evidence of effectiveness, it is well established that the effect shown in the adequate 240 and well-controlled trial must be, in FDA’s judgment, clinically meaningful. 30 , 31 This 241 determination depends on the relevance of the endpoint (see section III.A) and the magnitude of 242 the estimated treatment effect. For example, in a large trial, a small, statistically significant result 243 may be detected; however, depending on the outcome being evaluated, that small treatment 244 effect may not be clinically meaningful. On the other hand, even small effects may be clinically 245 meaningful when the effect is on survival or irreversible morbidity. 246
candidates.context: The persuasiveness of the trial results also depends on the findings for additional relevant 248 endpoints, as consistency across endpoints that reflect distinct and meaningful aspects of health 249 can increase confidence in results. In addition, the robustness of findings to violations in 250 assumption of the key analyses is important. For example, sensitivity analyses showing that 251 conclusions hold up on all plausible missing data assumptions help support the strength of 252 evidence from a trial. 253

candidates.statement: The persuasiveness and interpretation of an individual trial’s results should also be considered in 257 the context of the overall drug development program. In many programs, various objectives such 258 as finding an appropriate dose, studying different patient populations (e.g., with greater and 259 lesser disease severity, pediatric and adult populations, pregnant women), or comparing the drug 260 to other therapy will result in more than one trial providing data relevant to the evaluation of 261 effectiveness. The information generated in early-phase trials (e.g., supporting the drug’s 262 mechanism and selected dose), as well as any relevant external information (e.g., about the 263 disease pathophysiology and natural history, effects of the drug in related diseases, or effects of 264 drugs with similar mechanisms of action), can inform the expectations that the drug will be 265 effective prior to conducting an adequate and well-controlled trial. Such information is relevant 266 because the probability of erroneous conclusions of effectiveness depends on the prior 267 probability of effectiveness, the power, and the type I error probability. 32

candidates.statement: This section describes various approaches for designing high-quality development programs that 280 can support a demonstration of substantial evidence of effectiveness. 33 With any approach, it is 281 critical to consider the many factors described above that can impact the strength of evidence of 282 effectiveness. Sponsors should discuss their proposed approach with FDA early in development 283 and no later than at the end-of-phase 2 meeting. 284

candidates.statement: FDA will consider many factors in assessing whether one adequate and well-controlled trial plus 289 confirmatory evidence is sufficient for demonstrating substantial evidence of effectiveness. 290 These factors are expected to include the design, conduct, analysis, and persuasiveness of results 291 of the clinical trial; the source and strength of the confirmatory evidence; disease-specific 292 considerations (e.g., seriousness, unmet need, prevalence); and whether it is ethical and 293 practicable to conduct more than one adequate and well-controlled trial. The strength of the 294 design, conduct, analysis, and results of the single trial will affect the strength of confirmatory 295 evidence needed to establish substantial evidence of effectiveness. Given the lack of additional 296 adequate and well-controlled trials to substantiate results, FDA generally expects that a 297 demonstration of substantial evidence of effectiveness with this approach will involve a highly 298 persuasive trial or a source of strong confirmatory evidence (see discussion in sections IV.A.1 299 and IV.A.2 below). There may also be specific circumstances where additional regulatory 300 flexibility is considered in use of this approach (see section V). The approach of demonstrating 301 substantial evidence with one adequate and well-controlled trial plus confirmatory evidence 302 should be discussed with FDA prior to initiating the single trial. 303

If the applicant owns or has a right of reference to the data concerning the other drug, then the legal and regulatory concerns may be satisfied. If there is not such permission, for an NDA, reliance on FDA’s finding of safety and effectiveness for another drug may convert the application to a section 505(b)(2) application. A section 505(b)(2) application is subject to certain legal and regulatory requirements, which can include submission of patent certification(s) or statement(s) and delay in its submission or approval in accordance with the statutory exclusivity provisions, as applicable. See the draft guidance for industry Applications Covered by Section 505(b)(2) (October 1999). When final this guidance will represent the FDA’s current thinking on this topic.

candidates.statement: These clinical considerations should not be considered individually, but rather holistically, as 486 more than one consideration will often be relevant. For example, many rare diseases are life- 487 threatening and lack available therapy. In general, all relevant clinical considerations (e.g., 488 disease severity, unmet need, and disease rarity) should inform the extent and types of 489 flexibilities that may be appropriate. For example, certain flexibilities might be more acceptable 490 for a rare disease that is life-threatening and lacks available therapies than another rare disease 491 with less severe consequences with multiple therapeutic options already available. Both of these 492 scenarios, however, present a very different clinical context than a common, nonserious disease 493 with several available treatment options. However, in all scenarios, whether the disease is rare or 494 common, fatal or less severe clinically, substantial evidence of effectiveness must be 495 demonstrated. 496

candidates.statement: In certain clinical circumstances, some flexibility in success criteria for the primary statistical 520 analysis may also be acceptable. For example, in a trial relying on null hypothesis significance 521 testing, a significance level higher than the common one-sided 0.025 level may be acceptable in 522 some cases. The success criteria should be prespecified, justified, and agreed upon with the 523 Agency. The choice of success criteria should consider a variety of factors that impact the 524 consequences of false positive and false negative conclusions, such as the factors described 525 above (see section V.A) and the feasibility of different trial designs and sample sizes (e.g., the 526 degree to which studies of different sizes and with different significance levels would be 527 adequately powered to detect meaningful effect sizes). 528

candidates.statement: For example, mechanistic evidence of the drug’s treatment effect in a particular disease may be 542 appropriate to use as confirmatory evidence. Mechanistic evidence might be generated with a 543 clinical trial of a pharmacodynamic endpoint or with nonclinical studies. The pathophysiology of 544 the disease should be well-understood, and the drug’s mechanism of action should be both 545 clearly understood and shown to directly target the major driver(s) of the disease 546 pathophysiology. An example might be when the disease is caused by a single gene and/or 547 enzyme defect, and the drug’s mechanism of action corrects the enzymatic or genetic defect or 548 its sequelae. 549

candidates.statement: In certain circumstances, natural history data may also provide confirmatory evidence. For 551 example, a single randomized controlled trial showing marked improvement in survival could be 552 supported by data from separate sources (e.g., a natural history study or registry) that 553 demonstrate a very limited median survival time without treatment. The natural history data 554 would provide reassurance that the outcomes observed in the control group of the trial accurately 555 reflect those that would have been expected in the absence of the intervention. Natural history 556 data being used as confirmatory evidence should be distinct from any data used as a control for 557 the single adequate and well-controlled trial. Leveraging natural history data may involve use of 558 real-world data (RWD) sources. Whether an RWD source may be appropriate to provide 559 confirmatory evidence depends on several factors, such as the reliability and relevance of the 560 RWD source for its proposed use and, when relevant, the appropriateness of the study design and 561 the use of appropriate prespecified statistical methods and analyses. 43

candidates.statement: An FDA approval decision, among other things, requires a determination that a drug is safe for 575 its intended use, which involves assessing whether the benefits of the drug outweigh its risks. 576 Detailed considerations for the safety evaluation and benefit-risk assessment 44 are beyond the 577 scope of this guidance. However, it is important to note that sponsor development programs 578 should be planned to both demonstrate effectiveness and support an appropriate safety and 579 benefit-risk assessment. In some cases, adequate and well-controlled trial(s) that are sufficient to 580 demonstrate effectiveness may not include a sufficient number of participants or a sufficient 581 treatment duration to conclude that the drug is safe for its intended use. A larger or longer trial or 582 an additional trial may be needed to ensure a safety database of adequate size and duration to 583 support an appropriate benefit-risk assessment and drug approval.
